question: A security engineer is investigating a malware infection that has spread across a set of Amazon EC2 instances. A key indicator of the compromise is outbound traffic on TCP port 2905 to a set of command and control hosts on the internet. The security engineer creates a network ACL rule that denies the identified outbound traffic. The security engineer applies the network ACL rule to the subnet of the EC2 instances. The security engineer must identify any EC2 instances that are trying to communicate on TCP port 2905. Which solution will identify the affected EC2 instances with the LEAST operational effort?

options.A: Create a Network Access Scope in Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer. Use the Network Access Scope to identify EC2 instances that try to send traffic to TCP port 2905.
options.B: Enable VPC flow logs for the VPC where the affected EC2 instances are located. Configure the flow logs to capture rejected traffic. In the flow logs, search for REJECT records that have a destination TCP port of 2905.
options.C: Enable Amazon GuardDuty. Create a custom GuardDuty IP list to create a finding when an EC2 instance tries to communicate with one of the command and control hosts. Use Amazon Detective to identify the EC2 instances that initiate the communication.
options.D: Create a firewall in AWS Network Firewall. Attach the firewall to the subnet of the EC2 instances. Create a custom rule to identify and log traffic from the firewall on TCP port 2905. Create an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter to identify firewall logs that reference traffic on TCP port 2905

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amazon VPC Network Access Analyzer evaluates network access paths against configured scopes to verify whether reachability matches intent. It does not capture live traffic or identify which instances are actually attempting connections that were rejected on TCP port 2905.
explanations.B: Correct. VPC flow logs configured to capture rejected traffic will record the traffic denied by the network ACL, including the destination port. Searching the flow logs for REJECT records with a destination TCP port of 2905 directly identifies the affected EC2 instances with the least operational effort.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enabling GuardDuty with a custom IP list and then using Amazon Detective to trace the source requires extra configuration and additional services for analysis. This adds operational complexity and does not meet the least-operational-effort requirement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deploying AWS Network Firewall, writing a custom rule, and building a CloudWatch Logs metric filter is more complex to set up and maintain than simply reading VPC flow logs. It does not meet the least-operational-effort requirement.

question: A security engineer uses Amazon Macie to scan a company ʼ s Amazon S3 buckets for sensitive data. The company has many S3 buckets and many objects stored in the S3 buckets. The security engineer must identify S3 buckets that contain sensitive data and must perform additional scanning on those S3 buckets. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?

options.A: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication CRR) on the S3 buckets to replicate the objects to a second AWS Region. Configure Macie in the second Region to scan the replicated objects daily.
options.B: Create an AWS Lambda function as an S3 event destination for the S3 buckets. Configure the Lambda function to start a Macie scan of an object when the object is uploaded to an S3 bucket.
options.C: Configure Macie automated discovery to continuously sample data from the S3 buckets. Perform full scans of the S3 buckets where Macie discovers sensitive data.
options.D: Configure Macie scans to run on the S3 buckets. Aggregate the results of the scans in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Use the DynamoDB table for queries.

explanations.A: Incorrect. S3 Cross-Region Replication is intended for data redundancy and disaster recovery, not for optimizing sensitive-data discovery. Running Macie in a second Region to scan replicated objects adds cost and complexity and does not reduce administrative overhead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Triggering a Macie scan from a Lambda function on every object upload requires per-object invocation and does not scale well for many buckets and objects. This increases administrative overhead rather than reducing it.
explanations.C: Correct. Macie automated discovery continuously samples data across the S3 buckets to identify which buckets contain sensitive data, minimizing manual effort. You then run full scans only on the buckets where Macie discovered sensitive data, meeting the requirement with the least administrative overhead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aggregating scan results into an Amazon DynamoDB table only addresses storing and querying results; it adds extra steps and complexity and does not reduce the administrative overhead of identifying which buckets contain sensitive data.

question: A security engineer for a large company is managing a data processing application used by 1,500 subsidiary companies. The parent and subsidiary companies all use AWS. The application uses TCP port 443 and runs on Amazon C2 behind a Network Load Balancer NLB . For compliance reasons, the application should only be accessible to the subsidiaries and should not be available on the public internet. To meet the compliance requirements for restricted access, the engineer has received the publicand private CIDR block ranges for each subsidiary. What solution should the engineer use to implement the appropriate access restrictions for the application?

options.A: Create a NACL to allow access on TCP port 443 from the 1,500 subsidiary CIDR block ranges. Associate the NACL to both the NLB and EC2 instances.
options.B: Create an AWS security group to allow access on TCP port 443 from the 1,500 subsidiary CIDR block ranges. Associate the security group to the NLCreate a second security group for EC2 instances with access on TCP port 443 from the NLB security group.
options.C: Create an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service in the parent company account attached to the NLB. Create an AWS security group for the instances to allow access on TCP port 443 from the AWS PrivateLink endpoint. Use AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints in the 1,500 subsidiary AWS accounts to connect to the data processing application.
options.D: Create an AWS security group to allow access on TCP port 443 from the 1,500 subsidiary CIDR block ranges. Associate the security group with EC2 instances.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Network ACLs are stateless and would require managing return-traffic rules for 1,500 CIDR ranges, which is complex and hard to maintain. A network ACL also cannot be associated directly with a Network Load Balancer, and CIDR-based rules do not prevent public internet exposure by identity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although security groups are stateful, maintaining rules for 1,500 subsidiary CIDR ranges is complex and difficult to maintain, and security groups cannot provide the private, cross-account access model the compliance requirement calls for.
explanations.C: Correct. Creating an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service on the NLB in the parent account, and having the 1,500 subsidiaries connect through interface VPC endpoints in their own accounts, provides private cross-account access without exposing the application to the public internet. A security group on the instances can further restrict access to the PrivateLink endpoints.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Associating a security group that allows the 1,500 subsidiary CIDR ranges with the EC2 instances does not solve private cross-account access, and managing rules for 1,500 CIDR ranges is complex and hard to maintain.

question: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances. The company needs to continuously scan the EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Amazon Inspector. Set the scan mode to hybrid scanning.
options.B: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Enable the Malware Protection feature.
options.C: Use Amazon Inspector. Enable the Malware Protection feature.
options.D: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Enable the Runtime Monitoring feature.

explanations.A: Correct. Amazon Inspector is specifically designed for continuously scanning EC2 instances to detect software vulnerabilities and network exposure. Hybrid scanning mode combines agent-based and agentless scanning approaches to comprehensively cover vulnerability detection needs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amazon GuardDuty is primarily used for threat detection, such as malicious activity and anomalous behavior, not specifically for vulnerability scanning. Malware Protection is a GuardDuty feature focused on detecting malware, not scanning for software vulnerabilities or network exposure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While Amazon Inspector is the correct service choice, Malware Protection is not a feature of Amazon Inspector. Inspector's primary functions are vulnerability scanning and network exposure detection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amazon GuardDuty's primary function is threat detection, not vulnerability scanning or network exposure detection. Runtime Monitoring is used to monitor threats in running container and EC2 workloads, not for software vulnerability scanning.

question: A company has a requirement that no Amazon EC2 security group can allow SSH access from the CIDR block 0.0.0.0/0. The company wants to monitor compliance with this requirement at all times and wants to receive a near-real-time notification if any security group is noncompliant. A security engineer has configured AWS Config and will use the restricted-ssh managed rule to monitor the security groups. What should the security engineer do next to meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure AWS Config to send its configuration snapshots to an Amazon S3 bucket. Create an AWS Lambda function to run on a PutEvent to the S3 bucket. Configure the Lambda function to parse the snapshot for a compliance change to the restricted-ssh managed rule. Configure the Lambda function to send a notification to an Amazon Simple Notification Service Amazon SNS) topic if a change is discovered.
options.B: Configure an Amazon EventBridge event rule that is invoked by a compliance change event from AWS Config for the restricted-ssh managed rule. Configure the event rule to target an Amazon Simple Notification Service Amazon SNS) topic that will provide a notification.
options.C: Configure AWS Config to push all its compliance notifications to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configure a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the AWS Config log group to look for a compliance notification change on the restricted-ssh managed rule. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the metric filter to send a notification to an Amazon Simple Notification Service Amazon SNS) topic if the alarm is in the ALARM state.
options.D: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the CloudWatch metric for the restricted-ssh managed rule. Configure the CloudWatch alarm to send a notification to an Amazon Simple Notification Service Amazon SNS) topic if the alarm is in the ALARM state.

explanations.A: Incorrect. AWS Config generates configuration snapshots periodically rather than in real time, so parsing snapshots from an S3 bucket cannot deliver the near-real-time notification required. It also adds custom parsing logic and unnecessary complexity.
explanations.B: Correct. AWS Config integrates directly with Amazon EventBridge, which captures compliance change events in near real time. An EventBridge rule that matches the compliance change for the restricted-ssh managed rule and targets an Amazon SNS topic provides the near-real-time notification with minimal configuration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pushing AWS Config compliance notifications to CloudWatch Logs and then using a metric filter and alarm requires additional configuration and can introduce notification delay, so it does not reliably meet the near-real-time requirement and adds complexity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. AWS Config managed rules do not publish a native CloudWatch metric for the restricted-ssh rule, so you cannot configure a CloudWatch alarm directly on such a metric. This approach does not match how AWS Config reports compliance.
